extracted.intended_audience: writers and editors (general and professional), including legal and academic writers
extracted.subtask_short: editing for grammar, usage, and bias-free language
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing correct word forms, usages, and punctuation, and for producing bias-free language in polished American English. Includes many single-word usage entries, techniques for gender-neutral language, and punctuation rules (fonts, spacing, placement relative to quotes, URLs, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: slew / slough / slue usage distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between slew (/sloo/) meaning many or lots, slough meaning a grimy swamp (/sloo/ or /slow/), slough (/slaf/) meaning to discard, slewing (verb) meaning to turn or slide violently, and slue as an American variant of slewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct word by sense and pronunciation; note etymological differences and variant spellings (slue for present-tense verb in American English). Examples: 'you have a slew of cattle'; 'the car keeps slewing sideways'; 'Cain slew Abel'.

rubrics_metrics.name: slow vs slowly
rubrics_metrics.description: Both can be adverbs, but slowly is generally preferred for adverbial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'go slowly' in formal prose, though 'go slow' is common colloquial/injunction usage ('go slow!', 'take it slow'). See related guidance 5.160.

rubrics_metrics.name: sneak conjugation
rubrics_metrics.description: The verb sneak is conjugated regularly: sneak-sneaked-sneaked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'snuck' for dialectal or tongue-in-cheek usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: space (figurative) avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: The figurative use of space as 'area' has become voguish and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more specific words like 'area' rather than 'space' when used figuratively ('move into that space' discouraged).

rubrics_metrics.name: spit inflection by meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Different past forms depending on sense: as 'to expectorate' use spit-spat-spit; as 'to skewer' use spit-spitted-spitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inflect according to sense: 'he spat a curse' vs 'the hens have been spitted for broiling'.

rubrics_metrics.name: staunch vs stanch
rubrics_metrics.description: Staunch is an adjective meaning 'ardent and faithful'; stanch is a (American) verb meaning 'to stop the flow' (often bleeding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'staunch' for loyal/faithful (a staunch supporter) and 'stanch' to mean stop flow ('stanch the bleeding'); note British usage often uses 'staunch' as verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: stationary vs stationery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stationary = immobile; stationery = writing materials (paper and envelopes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember -er in stationery associates with 'paper'/'-er' in paper; mnemonic: stationer sells stationery.

rubrics_metrics.name: strait vs straight
rubrics_metrics.description: Strait = narrow channel or figuratively a difficult position ('dire straits'); straight = unbent, steady, sober, candid, honest, or heterosexual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'strait' in compounds meaning constriction (straitlaced, straitjacket); use 'straight' in other senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: strata plural usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Strata is the plural of stratum and should be kept plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double plural 'stratas' ('Fussell identified nine discrete strata').

rubrics_metrics.name: strategy vs tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategy is a long-term plan to achieve a goal; tactic is a short-term method to achieve an immediate limited success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strategy may involve several tactics; distinguish from stratagem (different spelling).

rubrics_metrics.name: such replacing this/that (legalese warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'such' to replace 'this' or 'that' (e.g., 'such building was later condemned') is symptomatic of legalese and is not more precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'such' only when meaning 'of that type' or 'of this kind' with mass or plural nouns ('such impudence'); otherwise prefer the, this, that, these, those.

rubrics_metrics.name: supersede spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Supersede derives from Latin sedeo; avoid variant spelling 'supercede'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'supersede' not 'supercede'.

rubrics_metrics.name: systematic vs systemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic = according to a plan or method; systemic = affecting the whole of something (often physiological).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'systemic' only for whole-system effects (systemic disease) or metaphorically for entire systems; use 'systematic' for organized methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: tantalizing vs titillating
rubrics_metrics.description: Tantalizing = tormenting by being just out of reach; titillating = tickling pleasantly, often with sexual connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the word by its connotation; 'tantalizing' implies desire without attainment; 'titillating' implies pleasurable arousal.

rubrics_metrics.name: text (verb) inflection
rubrics_metrics.description: As a verb, text is inflected regularly: text-texted-texted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the uninflected 'text' for past-tense forms (use 'texted').

rubrics_metrics.name: that vs which (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: In polished American prose, 'that' is used restrictively to narrow a category; 'which' is used nonrestrictively to add information about an already-identified item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'which' nonrestrictively usually preceded by comma/parenthesis/dash; use 'which' restrictively only when preceded by a preposition ('the situation in which we find ourselves'). The distinction is useful for clarity. Note British English often does not observe this distinction. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: there / their / they're distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: There = place/direction; their = possessive pronoun; they're = contraction of they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct form in context ('stay there', 'all their good wishes', 'they're calling now').

rubrics_metrics.name: therefore vs therefor
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore = 'as a result'; therefor (legalism) = 'for it' or 'for them'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'therefore' in ordinary prose; reserve 'therefor' for specific legal contexts ('received a refund therefor').

rubrics_metrics.name: thus (flat adverb) not thusly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'thus' (flat adverb); avoid 'thusly'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related guidance 5.160.

rubrics_metrics.name: till preposition/conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Till is a perfectly good preposition/conjunction; it is not a contraction of until and should not be written '’til'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'till' where appropriate; avoid '’til'.

rubrics_metrics.name: timbre vs timber
rubrics_metrics.description: Timbre = tonal quality of sound; timber = wood/trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'timbre' for musical sense and 'timber' for wood-related senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: tolerance vs toleration
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerance = habitual quality; toleration = a particular instance of being tolerant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose according to whether you mean a general disposition (tolerance) or a specific act (toleration).

rubrics_metrics.name: tortious vs tortuous vs torturous
rubrics_metrics.description: Tortious = relating to torts (legal wrongs); tortuous = full of twists and turns; torturous = involving severe suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the precise term to avoid confusion ('tortious interference' vs 'tortuous path' vs 'torturous exam').

rubrics_metrics.name: toward vs towards (American preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: In American English, 'toward' (without -s) is preferred; British English often uses 'towards'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For consistency, many American editors prefer the shorter forms without final s for directional words (upward, downward, forward, backward).

rubrics_metrics.name: transcript vs transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcript = written record or official student record; transcription = the act/process of creating a transcript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the noun vs process term appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: transpire senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally 'transpire' meant 'to come to be known'; now commonly also means 'happen' or 'occur'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware newer sense may smell like jargon; consider context if pretentious tone is a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: triumphal vs triumphant
rubrics_metrics.description: Triumphal refers to things made to celebrate victory (a triumphal arch); triumphant describes people feeling pride after victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'triumphal' for objects/celebrations, 'triumphant' for people.

rubrics_metrics.name: turbid vs turgid vs torpid
rubrics_metrics.description: Turbid = thick/opaque or figuratively 'unclear'; turgid = swollen or 'pompous/bombastic' (turgid prose); torpid = idle, lazy, sleepy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinct meanings to avoid misuse in figurative language.

rubrics_metrics.name: unexceptional vs unexceptionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexceptional = not very good; unexceptionable = not open to objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose carefully, they are not interchangeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: unique (reserve for one-of-a-kind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve 'unique' for the literal sense 'one of a kind' and avoid modifiers like 'very unique', 'more unique'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid degree modifiers on 'unique'; see related entry 5.89.

rubrics_metrics.name: unlawful / illegal / illicit / criminal gradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms are listed in ascending order of negative connotation: unlawful (may be morally innocent), illegal (formally condemned), illicit (evokes moral degeneracy), criminal (most severe). The first three can apply to civil wrongs; criminal implies crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word by degree of moral/legal condemnation intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: use vs utilize
rubrics_metrics.description: Use is usually best for simplicity; utilize is often overblown but can mean 'to use to best effect'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'use' except where 'utilize' conveys a distinct sense of employing advantageously ('how to utilize our staff most effectively').

rubrics_metrics.name: venal vs venial
rubrics_metrics.description: Venal (person) = mercenary/open to bribery; venal (thing) = purchasable. Venial = pardonable/trivial fault or sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between corruption (venal) and minor, forgivable faults (venial).

rubrics_metrics.name: verbal vs oral
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal = put into words (covers written and spoken); oral = conveyed through speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'oral' to specify spoken communication; 'verbal' can be ambiguous as it covers both.

rubrics_metrics.name: waive vs wave
rubrics_metrics.description: To waive = relinquish a claim; to wave = move to and fro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the two homophones.

rubrics_metrics.name: wangle vs wrangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrangle = argue angrily over time; wangle = obtain by cleverness/manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct verb for the intended meaning ('still wrangling over their parents’ estate' vs 'wangle last-minute tickets').

rubrics_metrics.name: wreak vs reek
rubrics_metrics.description: Wreak = cause harm or punish ('to wreak havoc'); past tense 'wreaked' (not wrought). Reek = stink (verb) or stench (noun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'wreak' for cause/punish and 'reek' for smell; avoid archaic 'wrought' as past of wreak.

rubrics_metrics.name: wrong vs wrongful distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong = immoral/unlawful or improper/incorrect; wrongful = unjust/unfair or unsanctioned by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use interchangeably; choose by intended nuance ('wrongful conduct' vs 'answers are wrong').

rubrics_metrics.name: who vs whom traditional rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Who = nominative (subject or predicate nominative); whom = objective (object of verb or preposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary trends: 'who' used colloquially even where 'whom' is traditional; avoid overcorrection (using whom incorrectly). For formal prose resist using 'who' indiscriminately but also avoid misusing 'whom'. See 5.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: whoever vs whomever (avoid whomever)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'whomever' unless certain of grammar; prefer 'whoever' or recast ('anyone who').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'whoever' in many contexts ('give this book to whoever wants it'); when uncertain, rephrase with anyone who.

rubrics_metrics.name: who's vs whose
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Who's' = contraction of 'who is'; 'whose' = possessive, and can refer to things as well as people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correctly to avoid confusion ('who's on first?' vs 'whose life is it'). See 5.64 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: workers' compensation preferred form
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'workers’ compensation' (not 'workmen’s compensation'); workers is always plural and hyphenate as phrasal adjective ('workers’-compensation system').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modern, inclusive form and correct hyphenation when adjectival.

rubrics_metrics.name: whether vs whether or not
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally use 'whether' alone; add 'or not' only when meaning 'regardless of whether'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'they didn’t know whether to go' not 'whether or not to go' unless 'regardless' sense intended ('we'll finish on time whether or not it rains').

rubrics_metrics.name: while for although/whereas (ambiguity warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: While can substitute for although or whereas in conversational tone but may be ambiguous because it also denotes time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When real ambiguity exists prefer 'although' or 'whereas' to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: whoever; whomever guidance (reiteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'whomever' unless certain; use 'anyone who' if unsure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated guidance to prefer simpler, less error-prone constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: your vs you're
rubrics_metrics.description: Your = possessive of you; you're = contraction of you are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct form to avoid common errors ('your class' vs 'you're welcome').

rubrics_metrics.name: maintaining credibility via bias-free language
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate biased language not central to meaning to maintain credibility with a wide readership; calling attention to absence of bias is also distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on readers' perception; avoid biased language unless central to meaning of the work. Aim for a style no reasonable person could call sexist but that doesn't contort language.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender bias: balancing approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid generic masculine pronoun and also avoid nontraditional gimmicks (he/she, s/he) or singular 'they' in formal prose if it sacrifices credibility with some readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware different readers have different sensitivities; choose techniques that preserve credibility for the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid other biases and stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid slighting allusions or stereotypes based on race, ethnicity, disability, religion, sexual orientation, transgender status, birth/family status, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful writers avoid language reasonable readers might find offensive or distracting, unless bias is central to meaning; suggest alternatives when editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: editor's responsibility on bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should point out biased terms or approaches, suggest alternatives, and ensure any retained biased language is retained by choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago editors don't maintain a strict banned-word list but apply reasoning case-by-case; aim for a style that neither hints at sexism nor contorts language to be nonsexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: techniques for achieving gender neutrality (nine methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nine suggested methods: (1) omit the pronoun; (2) repeat the noun; (3) use a plural antecedent; (4) use an article instead of a pronoun; (5) use 'one' (neutral singular); (6) use relative pronoun 'who'; (7) use the imperative mood; (8) use 'he or she' sparingly; (9) revise the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose combination that fits context. Each method includes examples and cautions (e.g., repeating nouns can irritate readers; 'he or she' should be used sparingly; rewrite if necessary). Use whichever produces clear, readable prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: use plural antecedent to avoid gendered pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: Making antecedent plural eliminates need for singular pronoun (e.g., 'contestants must conduct themselves').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of connotation change (individual duty vs collective responsibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: repeat the noun to avoid pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat the noun when the noun and pronoun are separated by many words to avoid awkward pronoun reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overuse; repeating more than twice or too soon suggests rewrite.

rubrics_metrics.name: use article instead of pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace singular personal pronoun with 'the' or 'a' when possible to avoid gendered pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often negligible effect on meaning and produces tighter sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: use neutral singular 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'one' as gender-neutral singular pronoun instead of gendered pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works well in many formal contexts ('an actor ... is likely to earn more than one in Paducah').

rubrics_metrics.name: use relative 'who' to replace pronoun after if
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace pronoun following 'if' with 'who' and revise the sentence as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps avoid gendered pronouns in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: use imperative mood to eliminate pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperative sentences remove need for explicit pronouns and can be useful in instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful in limited contexts (e.g., 'keep a close watch over children while monitoring the pool').

rubrics_metrics.name: use he or she in moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'he or she' sparingly, only when no other technique is satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating pronouns in same sentence; if that happens, rewrite the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: revise sentence when other techniques fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite sentences to eliminate need for personal pronouns when other techniques produce awkward phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show various rewrites to avoid 'his or her' constructions; degree of revision varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender-neutral singular pronouns caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional gender-neutral singular pronoun 'it' is inappropriate for humans; artifices like s/he and invented pronouns have not succeeded; singular 'they' gaining ground but not fully acceptable in formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless guidelines allow, be wary of using singular 'they' in formal contexts; for specific persons respect stated pronoun preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid problematic gender-specific suffixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate sex-specific suffixes (-ess, -ette) where possible; replace with suffix-free forms (author not authoress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious substituting '-person' for '-man' as it can sound pompous; prefer established alternatives (police officer, firefighter).

rubrics_metrics.name: use necessary gender-specific language when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When topic clearly concerns one sex or an inherently single-sex institution, gender-neutral phrasing may be inappropriate or produce absurd prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sex-specific terms when they accurately describe the subject (women’s studies, men’s golf, sorority).

rubrics_metrics.name: sex-specific labels as adjectives acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'woman' as modifier (woman judge) is acceptable and often preferable to 'lady' constructions; 'female' is often unobjectionable though may read biological in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use male/female as adjectives when parallel references require them ('834 male and 635 female officers').

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid other biased language: emphasize person-first
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the person rather than a characteristic (use 'Catholic man' not 'a Catholic' as noun label; 'child is deaf and mute' rather than 'deaf-mute child').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrelevant references to characteristics (sex, race, disability, age, etc.) unless they help reader develop a picture; use care to avoid unintended implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation governed by function and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation should promote ease of reading by clarifying relationships within and between sentences; apply consistent principles to avoid subjective obscuring of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles based on logical application of traditional U.S. practice; note exceptions and special requirements for other languages, math, citations, indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation and italics: use surrounding text font
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should appear in same font (roman or italic) as the main/surrounding text, except punctuation that belongs to a title in a different font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether punctuation belongs to surrounding sentence or to the italicized word/title; online/electronic formats may require attention to source tagging. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation and boldface/color: case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation following boldface or colored terms should be treated case-by-case depending on whether the punctuation belongs to the term or surrounding sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show mixed treatment; apply logic of ownership of punctuation to term vs sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation and font—print vs electronic aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional system places periods/commas/colons/semicolons in font of immediately preceding word if different; this is more aesthetic and reserved for print only. Electronic publications should prefer the logical system (punctuation matching surrounding sentence) because of tagging and typeface separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For print-only publications the aesthetic system may be used; for electronic works use the logical system described earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: parentheses and brackets font rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses and brackets should appear in the same font (roman or italic) as the surrounding text, not the material they enclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This system is easy and traditional; for printed works add thin space if italic letter touches roman parenthesis; for electronic works normally no adjustment. When a parenthetical phrase stands alone on its line, the parentheses/brackets are usually in same font as the phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: quotation marks font rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should appear in the same font as the surrounding text, which may differ from the font of the quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sentence or phrase in quotation marks appears on its own line, the quotation marks usually match that sentence/phrase font. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: one space between sentences (typeset matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: In typeset matter, use one space (not two) between two sentences and after a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a design layout calls for more space between elements, specify exact amount (e.g., em space). See 6.119-21 for spacing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation with URLs and email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences including email addresses or URLs should be punctuated normally; punctuation at sentence end belongs to the sentence for print readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angle brackets or wrappers are generally unnecessary in normal prose; hypertext markup should exclude surrounding punctuation. For line breaks of email/URL see 7.46.

rubrics_metrics.name: periods and commas precede closing quotation marks (US traditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods and commas go inside closing quotation marks whether double or single (traditional U.S. style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is longstanding U.S. practice (see table 6.1); exceptions and alternative systems (British) exist—see 6.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: colons and semicolons follow closing quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike periods and commas, colons and semicolons follow closing quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question marks and exclamation points may be inside or outside depending on whether they belong to the quoted matter; see table 6.1 and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: British alternative punctuation system
rubrics_metrics.description: British style often uses single quotation marks and includes in quotes only punctuation that appeared in original material; other punctuation follows closing quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are widespread; this system may be appropriate in textual criticism or technical/scientific settings. Use according to audience and conventions; see related sections.
